title: Accountability & Oversight
hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.
key_points: Accountability means officials must explain and answer for their decisions, and face consequences.
Vertical accountability runs to voters; horizontal accountability runs between state institutions.
Oversight tools include audits, independent watchdogs, ombudsmen, courts, and legislative inquiries.
A free press and transparency supply the information that makes accountability possible.
content_html: Every system that concentrates power faces the same risk: that those who hold it will use it carelessly, secretly, or for themselves. Accountability is the answer — the principle that officials must explain and justify what they do, and face real consequences when they abuse their position or fail in it. It is what keeps the grant of public power conditional rather than blank. But accountability does not happen by itself; it has to be built into institutions and continually exercised.
extra_html: It helps to distinguish two directions. Vertical accountability runs downward to the public: voters can reward or punish officials at elections, and citizens, journalists, and civil-society groups can demand answers in between. Horizontal accountability runs sideways, between institutions of the state: courts review the legality of actions, legislatures question and investigate the executive, auditors examine how public money was spent, and specialized watchdogs scrutinize conduct. One such institution is the ombudsman — an independent official who investigates citizens' complaints against the government — which Encyclopaedia Britannica describes as a now-widespread tool for checking maladministration. None of this works in the dark, which is why transparency and a free press are so central: accountability depends on information, on someone being able to find out what was actually done. Strong, layered oversight is the practical defense against corruption and abuse — and the absence of it is usually where both begin.

related.title: Political Corruption
related.hook: Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain — and it quietly drains a society, eroding trust, fairness, and the resources meant for everyone.

related.title: Checks and Balances
related.hook: Separating power isn't enough — each branch also gets tools to limit the others, so power keeps power in check.

related.title: The Free Press & Democracy
related.hook: A free press is sometimes called the "fourth estate" — an unofficial branch of power whose job is to watch the other three on the public's behalf.

flashcards.prompt: What does political accountability require of officials?
flashcards.back_html: That they explain and answer for their decisions — and face consequences for misconduct or failure.

flashcards.prompt: What is the difference between vertical and horizontal accountability?

choices.text: Vertical runs to voters; horizontal runs between state institutions
Vertical is local; horizontal is national
They mean exactly the same thing

flashcards.explanation_html: Voters holding officials to account is vertical; institutions checking one another (courts, audits, legislatures) is horizontal.

flashcards.prompt: Which is an oversight tool that helps enforce accountability?

choices.text: Independent audits, ombudsmen, courts, and legislative inquiries

flashcards.explanation_html: Audits, watchdogs, ombudsmen, courts, and inquiries are the machinery that scrutinizes officials and exposes wrongdoing.
